answer.rationale: The 18% cost mandate combined with incumbent's refusal to renegotiate leaves renewal or negotiation-only options insufficient. memory_c2 demonstrates that switching to the low-cost vendor achieved sharp unit cost reduction with quick onboarding and reliable invoicing—directly applicable to meeting the 18% target. memory_c4 shows negotiation can work, but only when the incumbent is willing; incumbent's refusal eliminates that path. Switching aligns with the cost objective while memory_c3 shows adding a second source mitigates single-point-of-failure risk. However, with 14 days to contract expiration and 94% line utilization, switching primary vendor is lower-risk than adding a second source (which requires dual qualification in compressed time). memory_c1 shows incumbent continuity has value, but not when the cost mandate cannot be met. A standard_experiment scale applies the low-cost vendor switch to this component cycle while retaining the option to dual-source or renegotiate at the next review if delivery performance flags. This preserves optionality and does not force a permanent vendor lock. The downstream risk is flagged: supply concentration increases temporarily until second-source qualification completes, but is mitigated by the vendor's prior track record and the assembly line's 6% buffer capacity.
